issues.legal_issue: A settlement deed that dedicates property to a public charity associated with Hindu religious festivals creates a specific endowment when its terms show that the settlor intended to divest himself and his heirs of the property.
material_facts: The deed described the property as allotted and reserved for charitable work and prohibited its sale or mortgage.
The settlor required his descendants to continue charitable activities at the property, including providing water and food to devotees during Hindu religious festivals.
The beneficiaries were devotees attending the festivals, an uncertain and fluctuating body of people.
The charitable activities were to be funded by the descendants from their business income; the deed did not dedicate income from the property.
The deed did not dedicate the property to the particular deity or give the temple control over the trust.
issues.conclusion: The deed created an absolute specific endowment for a public religious charity, not an endowment in favour of the particular deity. The property itself was endowed, although the deed did not endow money for the charity.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 6(19) of the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1959, a specific endowment includes property or money endowed for a specific service or charity in a temple or for another religious charity. Section 6(16) defines religious charity as a public charity associated with a Hindu festival or religious observance. Whether a deed effects complete dedication or merely imposes a charge is determined from the instrument as a whole and the settlor’s intention; the use of words such as trust or trustee is not decisive (Menakuru Dasaratharami Reddi v Duddukuru Subba Rao). A public charity benefits the public or an uncertain and fluctuating body, unlike a private charity benefiting identifiable individuals (Mahant Ram Saroop Dasji v S P Sahi; M J Thulasiraman v Hindu Religious & Charitable Endowment Admn). Association with a festival means connection or relation to it and does not require control by the authority administering the festival (Commr, Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments v Narayana Ayyangar; K S Soundararajan v Commr of Hindu Religious & Charitable Endowments). A public charity associated with a religious festival is a religious charity, and property endowed for that charity is a specific endowment (M J Thulasiraman).

rule.if: settlement_endowment_dispute and property_reserved_for_charity and heirs_obliged_to_continue_charity and beneficiaries_are_uncertain_public and charity_connected_to_hindu_festival

predicates.settlement_endowment_dispute: The proceeding concerned whether a settlement deed had dedicated property for charitable purposes.
predicates.property_reserved_for_charity: The settlor described the property as allotted or reserved for charity and restricted its alienation.
predicates.heirs_obliged_to_continue_charity: The settlor required descendants to continue charitable activities at the property.
predicates.beneficiaries_are_uncertain_public: The charity was for a changing, unidentifiable body of people rather than a fixed group of individuals.
predicates.charity_connected_to_hindu_festival: The charitable activities were carried out for devotees in connection with Hindu religious festivals.

issues.definition: When a settlement reserves property for continuing charity, benefits an uncertain public, and connects the charity to a Hindu festival, the property is a specific endowment for a public religious charity rather than for a particular deity.

issues.legal_issue: A specific endowment within the statutory definition is governed by the Act without a separate government notification extending the Act to a charitable endowment on grounds of mismanagement.
material_facts: The trust was a public charitable endowment associated with Hindu religious festivals and was found to be a specific endowment under the Act.
The trust argued that the Act did not apply because the government had not issued a notification extending its provisions to the trust.
There was no allegation that the trust was mismanaged or that the government had reason to believe it was mismanaged.
issues.conclusion: The Act applied to the specific endowment without a notification under Section 3. Section 3 concerns extending the Act to public charitable endowments in the circumstances specified there; it did not exclude this specific endowment from the Act.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3 of the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1959, provides a process for extending provisions of the Act to a Hindu or Jain public charitable endowment where the government has reason to believe it is being mismanaged and, after inquiry, considers extension necessary. A charitable endowment that independently satisfies the definition of a specific endowment in Section 6(19) is governed by the Act; it need not first be brought within the Act through Section 3.

predicates.act_coverage_disputed_for_lack_of_extens: A party disputed the application of the statutory scheme because no government notice had extended it to the charitable endowment.
predicates.endowment_is_specific: The property was endowed for a specific public religious charity associated with a Hindu festival.

issues.definition: When statutory coverage is challenged for lack of an extension notice but the endowment independently qualifies as specific, the Act applies without that notice.

issues.legal_issue: A civil court cannot authorize the sale of property forming part of an endowment regulated by the Act when the Act assigns approval of the sale to the statutory authority.
material_facts: The trust filed a civil suit seeking permission to sell part of the endowed property and deposit the sale proceeds in a bank.
The property formed part of a specific endowment regulated by the Act.
The Act provides for approval of an alienation by the Commissioner and requires prior government approval.
The civil courts below permitted the proposed sale, but the Supreme Court held that the suit was not maintainable.
issues.conclusion: The civil suit seeking permission for the sale was barred. The Commissioner was the appropriate authority to consider the proposed sale under the Act, and the trust remained at liberty to use the procedure prescribed by the Act.
issues.legal_principle: Section 108 of the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1959, bars suits or other legal proceedings concerning administration or management of a religious institution, or other matters for which the Act provides. Section 34 assigns sanction of an alienation of relevant immovable property to the Commissioner and requires prior government approval. The civil court therefore cannot grant the requested sale permission in place of the statutory process.

predicates.civil_suit_seeks_permission_to_sell_endo: A party brought a civil suit asking the court to permit the sale of property held for an endowment.
predicates.property_is_regulated_by_statutory_schem: The property formed part of an endowment governed by a statutory scheme.
predicates.statute_assigns_sale_approval_to_authori: The statutory scheme assigns approval of the proposed alienation to a designated authority.

issues.definition: When a civil suit seeks permission to sell property governed by a statutory endowment scheme that assigns sale approval to an authority, the civil court cannot authorize the sale.
